metadata.purpose: Real, genuine, thoughtful insights/hacks/strategies for parents planning summer + year-round enrichment for elementary and middle school kids.

sections.title: Registration window cheat sheet — when to actually book

items.label: December–January
items.detail: Member registration opens at top-tier museum/zoo camps in major metros (Pacific Science Center, Woodland Park Zoo, Burke Museum, Seattle Children's Theatre). Premium camps fill in days. If you're not yet a member, the membership pays for itself just from earlier access.

items.label: February (Early Bird windows)
items.detail: Camp Galileo Early Bird discount typically expires Feb 28 ($50/wk savings). YMCA Camp Orkila + Camp Sealth registration windows open this month — overnight camps. Multi-week discounts often stack with Early Bird.

items.label: March (general public registration)
items.detail: Most Seattle-metro institution camps open general (non-member) registration. Point Defiance Zoo & Aquarium typically opens early-mid March. Most popular sessions fill within 2-3 weeks.

items.label: April–May (last call + scholarship windows)
items.detail: Most popular sessions full. Off-the-radar specialty camps still have space. Scholarship application windows often close mid-May — check each org. Many districts publish their summer enrichment lists in April.

items.label: June (late game + cancellations)
items.detail: Some camps add late sessions if demand exists. Cancellation lists at premium camps move quickly — call directly, don't just check website. Parks dept rec camps almost always have space.

sections.title: Scholarship cheat sheet — generous aid most parents don't ask about

items.label: YMCA — sliding scale Price A / Price B
items.detail: All Y branches use a sliding-scale cost structure. You self-select based on household income. No documentation required at registration. Some Ys offer additional financial assistance beyond Price B — ask the membership desk directly. Camp Orkila and other residential Ys have the same structure.

items.label: Pacific Science Center — needs-based scholarships up to 100%
items.detail: Application opens early February (well before general registration). Scholarship windows are SEPARATE from regular registration — apply to both. Bring tax return + proof of income. 100% scholarships exist; partial more common.

items.label: Woodland Park Zoo — scholarships up to 100% in 20% increments
items.detail: Tiered based on income. Application is short. They publish the income brackets — check the FAQ. Apply once per year, valid for all WPZ camps that summer.

items.label: Camp Sealth (Camp Fire CPS) — Camperships
items.detail: Need-based aid called 'Camperships'. Apply 4-6 weeks before session. Particularly generous for 'first-time camper' families. Foster, kinship, and EBT/WIC families get expedited review.

items.label: Point Defiance Zoo — Pierce County resident aid
items.detail: Special scholarship pool for Pierce County residents on EBT/WIC/foster/kinship. Smaller pool but high acceptance rate if eligible.

items.label: Camp Galileo — financial aid + multi-week sibling discounts
items.detail: Up to 75% aid for qualifying families. Multi-week + multi-sibling discounts stack with aid. Apply early — pool is smaller than the museum/zoo programs.

items.label: School district summer programs — often free or near-free
items.detail: Most districts run summer enrichment using federal Title I funds. Eligibility may be income-tested or open to all district kids. Check your district's website starting in March. Often the BEST kept secret in the local market.

sections.title: Nationwide & remote programs — equally available to ANY family

items.label: iD Tech (online + in-person at universities)
items.detail: Coding, game dev, robotics, AI. Online courses for ages 7-19 (live instructor, small groups). In-person held at 50+ university campuses nationwide. Pricing high but financial aid available. Best-known brand in tech ed for kids.

items.label: Camp Galileo (CA + WA expansion + virtual)
items.detail: Also offers Galileo Online — interactive virtual camps for ages 5-12. Project-based, not video lectures. Lower cost than in-person.

items.label: Camp Invention (National Inventors Hall of Fame)
items.detail: Run at thousands of host elementary schools nationwide each summer. STEM + creativity, ages K-6. Pricing modest. Search by zip on their website to find a host school near you.

items.label: Khan Academy Kids + Camps
items.detail: Free K-2 app year-round. Some library systems run Khan-aligned summer programs. Cheapest meaningful enrichment option for early elementary.

items.label: Outschool — small-group online classes (K-12)
items.detail: Marketplace of online classes from independent teachers. Subjects from D&D club to coding to creative writing. Per-class pricing, often $10-30/session. Great for kids with niche interests not served by local options.

items.label: MIT Beaver Works Summer Institute (online + Cambridge)
items.detail: Free for accepted students. Targeted at rising 10th-12th but worth knowing about for 7th-8th graders to plan toward.

items.label: AoPS (Art of Problem Solving) Online Math
items.detail: Math classes from Beast Academy (grades 2-5) through advanced HS competition prep. Online or self-paced. The serious math kid pipeline.

items.label: DigiPen Open World Summer Workshops (online + Redmond)
items.detail: Game design, animation, programming. Ages 5-12 + teen tracks. Strong instruction quality.

items.label: MOOC platforms — Coursera, edX, Khan Academy
items.detail: Free university-level content available to motivated middle schoolers. Especially good for kids who finish their grade-level curriculum early.

items.label: Connections Academy + K12 — full virtual public school
items.detail: Free in many states. Year-round option not just summer. Worth considering for kids whose schools aren't a fit, or families with travel flexibility.

sections.title: Sleepaway readiness — is your kid actually ready?

items.label: Green-light signals (start considering 3-5 day sessions)
items.detail: Has done overnights at friends' or relatives' houses without getting homesick. Asks about sleepaway camp themselves. Can dress, brush teeth, and manage basic hygiene independently. Comfortable being out of contact with parents for 24+ hours.

items.label: Yellow-light signals (try a shorter program first)
items.detail: Has had overnight successes but also some homesick episodes. Wants to go but parents are anxious. Manages most independence but needs reminders. Try a 2-3 day camp through the local Y or church first.

items.label: Red-light signals (wait a year)
items.detail: Has anxiety about overnights at relatives'. Has not asked about sleepaway. Struggles with morning routines independently. Nighttime fears or bedwetting still active. Don't push it. Plenty of strong day-camp options through age 12.

items.label: What sleepaway camps actually teach
items.detail: Independence in low-stakes context. Conflict resolution with peers (forced proximity surfaces it). Self-advocacy with adults outside parents. Managing physical fatigue + recovery. Comfort with discomfort (weather, basic accommodations). These compound across years.

items.label: First-timer success patterns
items.detail: Pre-write a few letters together (kids love getting mail). Pre-decide on a comfort item that's not too precious to lose. Talk through what a hard moment might look like + what the kid would do. Don't promise an early pickup — that signals 'this might fail' and erodes confidence.

sections.title: Budget framework — getting maximum value across the summer

items.label: The 60/30/10 frame (a starting heuristic)
items.detail: If you have a fixed summer budget: spend ~60% on a recurring 'anchor' — typically the YMCA / parks dept day camp 3-4 weeks running ($150-300/wk subsidized). Spend ~30% on 1-2 specialty experiences ($400-600 each — the museum camp, the coding camp, the zoo camp). Reserve ~10% for the wildcard — the niche experience the kid asked for, or a weekend mini-camp.

items.label: Multi-summer planning (K-8 arc)
items.detail: K-2: low-stakes exposure across many areas. Cheap day camps + lots of unstructured time. 3-5: discover sustained interests. Add specialty camps in 1-2 areas of demonstrated interest. 6-8: deepen + try sleepaway. Multi-week intensives or residential programs in the area of strongest interest.

items.label: When premium IS worth it
items.detail: When the program creates an experience the kid couldn't replicate at home (boats, horses, theatrical production with peers, 24/7 immersion). When the instructor is genuinely expert (you can tell from the bio + curriculum). When the kid has earned a 'next level' moment after years at lower tiers.

items.label: When premium is NOT worth it
items.detail: When you're paying for the campus brand more than the curriculum. When the kid would happily attend a comparable cheaper option. When you're stretching the family budget. When the kid is reluctantly attending.

items.label: Free + cheap that's actually great
items.detail: Public library summer reading programs (often have weekly events + prizes). Parks dept rec camps. School district summer enrichment (often free with district enrollment). Free museum/library passes (many libraries lend museum passes). Junior ranger badges at national parks ($0).

items.label: Over-stacking specialty camps
items.detail: 8 weeks of different 'enrichment' burns kids out. Mix in unstructured time. The downtime is when interests actually consolidate.

items.label: Treating it like college admissions
items.detail: K-8 summers don't appear in college applications. Picking based on 'what looks good' backfires — kids sense the inauthenticity and disengage.

items.label: Skipping the kid's preferences
items.detail: Kids who choose what to attend are happier, more engaged, more likely to develop sustained interests. Even a 6-year-old can rank options.

items.label: Assuming free=bad and expensive=good
items.detail: Parks dept day camps are often excellent. Premium camps are sometimes just well-marketed.

items.label: Not asking about scholarships
items.detail: Most reputable orgs have 50-80% aid available; rarely advertised. Email the camp director directly — application is often shorter than expected.

items.label: Sleepaway too early
items.detail: Pushing a 6-year-old into a week-long overnight because the parent went themselves at that age. Different kid, different generation. Honor the readiness signals.

items.label: Single-track specialization too early
items.detail: A kid who does only soccer camps every summer K-8 won't necessarily play in HS. Variety in K-5 → emerging interest in 6-8 → specialization in 9-12 is the healthier arc.

items.label: Trade with a friend's family for week-long swap
items.detail: Two families with similar-aged kids each take one week of the other family's kid. Effectively 'free childcare' for a week, kids get the friend-immersion they love, and both families get a week of fewer mouths to feed. Works best ages 7+.

items.label: Volunteer-as-CIT (Counselor In Training) at age 12-14
items.detail: Many camps need junior counselors. Tweens get free or discounted attendance + leadership experience. Apply early — these slots fill faster than camper slots. YMCA, Camp Fire, BGCA all have CIT pipelines.

items.label: Subscribe to a museum at the right tier
items.detail: Not all memberships are equal. Look for the tier that includes 'priority camp registration' — usually $150-200 family-tier upgrade. Pays for itself just from earlier access to popular camps.

items.label: ACA accreditation is a real signal
items.detail: American Camp Association accreditation means health/safety/staff-ratio standards verified annually. Not a fancy badge — actually means something. Free filter at acacamps.org/find-a-camp.

items.label: University youth programs — often hidden gems
items.detail: UW Robinson Center, DigiPen Open World, Stanford EPGY (now Compass), Northwestern Center for Talent Development. Often more substantive than for-profit camps. Check your local research university.

items.label: City parks dept after-school + summer = often the best deal
items.detail: Seattle Parks, Bellevue Parks, Tacoma Metro Parks all run summer day camps for $20-50/day. Quality varies by site, not by department. Visit a site mid-program to assess.

items.label: The 'kid needs a break' permission slip
items.detail: If the kid hasn't had unstructured outdoor time in months, schedule 1-2 unprogrammed weeks. Sounds counterintuitive but kids who get 'permission' to be bored often emerge with new self-directed interests. The opposite of camp.

items.label: Sibling camps at the same site = parent sanity
items.detail: Big multi-program sites (YMCA, large day camps) can take siblings of different ages at once. One drop-off, one pickup, one schedule. Massive parental QoL upgrade vs juggling 3 different camps in 3 locations.

items.label: International summer = often cheaper than US specialty camps
items.detail: Language immersion programs in Mexico/Costa Rica/Spain for ages 8-14 can run $1500-3000 for 2 weeks INCLUDING flights. Compare to a $700/week US specialty camp. Best for kids with at least basic Spanish/French foundation.

items.label: Theater + arts intensives often have surprise scholarships
items.detail: Most regional theaters with kids' programs (Seattle Children's Theatre, ACT Theatre, etc.) have under-applied-for scholarship pools. Even a no-pretense email asking about aid often surfaces options not on the website.

sections.title: From the field — fresh insider notes (auto-discovered)

items.label: Math Kangaroo USA — Late-fee penalty is nearly 2x
items.detail: Math Kangaroo USA charges $18 for standard registration (Sep 15 - Dec 31) but jumps to $35 if you wait until Jan 1 - Feb 1 — almost double. The contest is the same. (As of 2026-04-26.) Test day 2026 is Mar 19.

items.label: MOEMS — Individual students cannot enroll directly
items.detail: MOEMS Math Olympiad only accepts SCHOOL TEAMS, not individual students. If a school does not run MOEMS, parents need to organize through a homeschool co-op, after-school program, or PTA. 2026-27 enrollment opens May 2026.

items.label: KiwiCo — Annual plan saves ~25-30% over monthly
items.detail: KiwiCo monthly is ~$24/mo but the 12-month plan drops to ~$18.50/mo (save ~$66/yr per child) and 6-month to ~$19.95/mo. Many parents subscribe month-to-month and miss this; the discount is on the same crates.

items.label: MEL Science — First box 60% off during promo windows
items.detail: MEL Science runs first-box 60%-off promos during Black Friday, Cyber Monday, and parts of summer — drops month-1 cost from $29.90 to ~$12. Annual plan is also '12 months for the price of 8' — equivalent to ~33% off.

items.label: ChessKid — Free tier covers everything that matters for under-rated kids
items.detail: ChessKid Gold is $49/yr for lessons + puzzles, but FREE tier already includes unlimited play, slow chess, basic puzzles, and the FunMaster Mike video series. Most kids under USCF 800 don't need Gold. Many local chess clubs sponsor Gold memberships for active club members.

items.label: Prodigy Math — Paid tiers are 100% cosmetic, not content
items.detail: Prodigy Math Level Up ($9.95/mo) and Ultimate ($14.95/mo) DO NOT unlock any additional math content — all 45,000+ curriculum-aligned questions are free. Paid tiers only unlock cosmetic upgrades, member zones, and progress dashboards. Don't pay unless your child specifically motivates around the rewards.

items.label: Steve & Kate's Camp — auto-refund unused passes is unusual leverage
items.detail: Buy 15+ Day Passes ($114/day) instead of a Summer Pass; unused passes are AUTOMATICALLY refunded after summer. Most parents over-buy fearing waste — this model removes that risk entirely. Bay Area + LA only.

items.label: Lawrence Hall of Science — 2-week sessions vs 1-week peers
items.detail: Lawrence Hall (UC Berkeley) deliberately runs 2-week sessions instead of the standard 1-week. Better content depth + camper community, but parents need to plan around the longer commit. $625–$950/wk; financial aid app is open for 2026.

items.label: California Science Center — half + afternoon = full day flexibility
items.detail: CSC Hands-On Science Camp lets you mix-and-match a morning class + afternoon class to make a full day. Extended care (8–9am & 3–5pm) is $110/wk for members vs $120 non — membership pays for itself if you need wraparound care all summer.

items.label: Birch Aquarium — Scripps scholarships are quietly available
items.detail: Birch Aquarium summer camps ($250–$600/wk) have needs-based scholarships not advertised on the main page. Email birchaquariumprogram@ucsd.edu BEFORE registration windows close — Scripps backs the program so funding is more reliable than a typical aquarium.

items.label: The Tech Interactive — IMAX + after-hours exhibits included
items.detail: CAMP at The Tech (rising grades 3–6) includes IMAX Dome films and exclusive after-hours exhibit access in tuition. Hidden value vs comparable 1-week STEM camps. 8 sessions June 15 – Aug 7, 2026; cost not on landing page — direct contact required.

items.label: Synthesis — Two products under one brand
items.detail: Synthesis sells two completely different products under the same brand: Synthesis Teams ($95/mo, ages 8-14, weekly cohort problem-solving) and Synthesis Tutor ($25-30/mo, K-5, AI math tutor). Many parents land on the wrong product page — verify which one you want before signing up. Tutor at synthesis.com/tutor vs cohort at synthesis.com/teams. Confirmed 2026-04-26.

items.label: Mathnasium — Summer pricing varies by franchise
items.detail: Same 8-session summer package can range $269-$349+ for elementary depending on location, and 2-hour sessions roughly double that ($538-$698 elementary). Always ask the local center for BOTH 1-hour AND 2-hour bundle quotes — per-hour rate often drops with the longer block. New-student summer enrollment fee $49 or $99 depending on package. Confirmed 2026-04-26.

items.label: Code Ninjas — Half-day blocks stack into full-day at one center
items.detail: Code Ninjas summer camps run as half-day blocks (8:30am-12pm OR 12:30pm-4pm). Stacking BOTH blocks at the same franchise gets you full-day coverage at one location — but it's not advertised on the booking page. Ask the local center to combine bookings, which often unlocks a small lunch-bridge accommodation. Confirmed 2026-04-26.

items.label: Connected Camps — 90 min/day, NOT a childcare solution
items.detail: Connected Camps' weeklong online courses are 90 minutes/day for 5 days — total 7.5 hours of instruction, not full-day camp. Excellent enrichment supplement (Minecraft, Roblox, esports, ages 8-13), but parents expecting daycare-equivalent coverage will be surprised. Pair with another program if you need full-day coverage. Confirmed 2026-04-26.

items.label: Outschool — Quality is per-teacher, not per-platform
items.detail: Outschool is a marketplace — Outschool keeps 30%, teachers set their own prices and curriculum. A 'great Outschool class' is really a great individual teacher. Sort by reviews, watch the teacher's intro video, check their other listings before enrolling. Class quality has more to do with the teacher than the Outschool brand. Confirmed 2026-04-26.

items.label: Brain Chase — Async + travel-friendly summer learning
items.detail: Brain Chase ($179 early bird / $199 standard) runs June 15 - July 17, 2026 — 5 weeks, ~4 hrs/week academic. Async pacing means kids can do it during summer travel; the global treasure-hunt narrative (real buried prize) wraps academic work as a quest. Best fit grades 2-8. Confirmed 2026-04-26.

items.label: Mystery Science — Free trial extended through June 30, 2026 (no card)
items.detail: Mystery Science (mysteryscience.com) currently has a free trial through June 30, 2026 with no credit card required, giving access to select K-5 units, mini-lessons, and hands-on activities. Best low-friction summer-science option for elementary parents to try before committing to a paid family plan (added 2026-04-26).

items.label: Generation Genius — Free trial is 14 days no-card, NOT 30
items.detail: Generation Genius (generationgenius.com) advertises a 14-day free trial that requires zero credit card upfront — easier-than-most onramp. After 14 days you must add payment to continue. Subscription pricing is not on the public landing — must email or visit /subscribe to see (added 2026-04-26).

items.label: Camp CrunchLabs — Auto-rolls into monthly at $27.45 after 12-week summer
items.detail: Camp CrunchLabs ships 12 weekly Build Boxes for $329.40 (~$27.45/wk), but at week 13 you are auto-enrolled into the regular Build Box month-to-month subscription at $27.45/month. Parents who want only the summer experience must cancel before the auto-renew (added 2026-04-26).

items.label: Camp Wonderopolis — Fully free with no payment ever (NCFL-funded)
items.detail: Camp Wonderopolis (camp.wonderopolis.org) by the National Center for Families Learning is 100% free, no credit card, no upgrade tier. Doesn't appear on most paid 'best summer camp' lists because there's nothing to monetize — but that's why it's a hidden gem for budget-conscious or homeschool families (added 2026-04-26).

items.label: Maker Camp — Library or makerspace cohort makes solo at-home much better
items.detail: Maker Camp (makercamp.make.co) is free and self-serve, but kids who do it alone at home often plateau by week 3. Look for a local library, science museum, or makerspace among the 2,000+ registered Maker Camp host sites worldwide — the cohort element transforms engagement (added 2026-04-26).

items.label: BrainPOP — 30-day free trial requires CC; cancel before day 30 to avoid charge
items.detail: BrainPOP's 30-day free trial requires a credit card upfront and auto-converts to the $129/yr family plan if not cancelled before day 30. Set a calendar reminder. The Grades 3-8 + Jr (K-3) combo at $159/yr is only $30 more if you have multiple kids — usually worth the upgrade (added 2026-04-26).

items.label: AAUW Tech Trek — $50 covers a $1,000+ residential STEM week
items.detail: AAUW Tech Trek (rising 8th-grade girls) is fully sponsored by AAUW donations — families pay only a nominal $50 fee + transportation, when the actual program cost runs $1,000+. Branches often waive even the $50 for families in need. Path is teacher/counselor nomination, NOT direct application — talk to your kid's 7th-grade STEM teacher in winter.

items.label: NSBE SEEK — open to all students, fully free, but selective
items.detail: Despite NSBE's name, SEEK 2026 (rising 4th-6th) is open to ALL students with demonstrated STEM interest — not Black-only. It's free with shipped materials. Selection is competitive (income, attendance, prior participation factor in). Register early via seek.nsbe.org; rolling admission until program starts.

items.label: Black Girls CODE — most participants pay $0 via sponsorship
items.detail: Black Girls CODE's 2026 Summer Camp 'She Won't Just Play the Game. She'll Build It' runs in 10 US cities + 2 virtual sessions. Most participants pay nothing — corporate sponsorship covers tuition. Open to all girls 10-17 (Black girls prioritized but not exclusive). Apply at wearebgc.org/summer-camp; competitive due to high demand.

items.label: Northwestern CTD Solstice — no district nomination required
items.detail: Common misconception: parents assume Northwestern CTD requires gifted-program district nomination. It does NOT. Eligibility is established directly via test scores or teacher recommendation through CTD's own application — open to any rising 4th-6th grader meeting the bar. Don't wait on the district.

items.label: Math Beasts Camp — placement is by readiness not strict grade
items.detail: AoPS Academy's Math Beasts Camp 2-5 align to fall grade by default, but placement is fluid. A kid finishing 2nd grade who's ready for harder material can be placed in Camp 3 — email the registrar before locking in. Distinct product from Beast Academy Online (self-paced curriculum).

items.label: CodeWizardsHQ — money-back guarantee does NOT cover summer camps
items.detail: CodeWizardsHQ promotes a 100% money-back guarantee for four sessions of their year-round structured tracks. The guarantee does NOT apply to summer camps — refund policy is much stricter. Read the fine print before booking summer-only sessions.

items.label: Juni Learning — 2-week free trial is the smart entry point
items.detail: Juni Learning's monthly fees run $140-$450+ depending on cadence/subject — but the 2-week free trial includes actual classes (often via placement or intro course). Use the trial to verify instructor fit before committing; their model is 1:1 so chemistry with the teacher matters more than at small-group competitors.

items.label: Seattle metro / Pacific Northwest
items.detail: Most camps run Jun 22 – Aug 28, 2026, Mon-Fri weekly. Week of Jun 29 - Jul 3 often runs 4-day (Mon-Thu) due to Jul 4 weekend. Some camps also run 4-day week of Jun 15 due to Juneteenth (Fri Jun 19).

items.label: Bay Area / SoCal
items.detail: Jun 15 – Aug 7, 2026. Schools out earlier than Pacific NW so summer programming starts/ends 1 week earlier. Examples: Lawrence Hall (Berkeley), CAMP at The Tech Interactive (San Jose), California Science Center (LA), Birch Aquarium (La Jolla) all run Jun 15 – Aug 7.

items.label: Chicago / Midwest
items.detail: Jun 29 – Aug 7, 2026 typical. Northwestern CTD (Evanston + Chicago South Loop) is the canonical anchor.

items.label: NYC
items.detail: Late June through late August. AMNH typical Jul 6 – Aug 21. Member registration February; general March-April.

items.label: Year-round / online programs
items.detail: No summer window — Khan, Beast Academy, Synthesis, Code.org, Mystery Science (free trial through Jun 30, 2026), Generation Genius, Khan, NASA STEM virtual, Nat Geo Kids. Treat sessionPattern as 'year-round-classes' and don't gate on summer dates.

items.label: Single-day / event-based
items.detail: Burke Museum (Dino Trackers Jul 13 confirmed; rest of program runs through summer). Apple Camp at Apple Stores Jul-Aug. UW Engineering Discovery Days is an annual 2-day spring event — not a summer program.

sections.title: Major Seattle / WA + select national camp reg timing (2026 confirmed)

items.label: YMCA Camp Orkila (overnight, Orcas Island)
items.detail: Registration opens Feb 4, 2026 at 6 a.m. Sessions 7-28 days, grades 3-12. Sliding scale (Price A/B); $50 deposit; financial assistance. Fills in days — set a calendar reminder.

items.label: Pacific Science Center Camps for Curious Minds
items.detail: Member early reg Feb 2; general public Feb 9. Scholarship apps open Feb 6 (separate from regular registration — apply to BOTH). Pay due in full by May 1 or balance auto-charged. 100+ themed weekly camps PreK-8 across 6 metro locations + new Bothell, Kenmore, Salish Sea.

items.label: Museum of Flight ACE (Aerospace Camp Experience)
items.detail: Member early reg Feb 20 11am PT, general public Feb 21 10am PT. K-9th grade. By April many K-3 sessions are at capacity (waitlist mode). Campership Program offers $100/$200/$300 financial aid. Contact ACE@museumofflight.org.

items.label: Camp Galileo Bellevue (STEAM Day Camp)
items.detail: Currently enrolling for Summer 2026. Early-Bird ends Feb 28 ($50/wk savings); rolling registration after. Multi-week + multi-sibling discounts stack. 9am-3pm M-F, optional extended care 8-9am + 3-6pm. Up to 75% need-based aid available.

items.label: Point Defiance Zoo & Aquarium (Tacoma)
items.detail: Member registration Mar 10 8am, general public Mar 12 8am. Combined zoo + aquarium campus camps for ages PreK-8. Pierce County resident scholarship pool for EBT/WIC/foster/kinship families.

items.label: Lawrence Hall of Science (UC Berkeley)
items.detail: Member registration opened late 2025; general public Jan 2, 2026 — earlier than most CA camps. 2-week sessions ($625-950/wk) instead of 1-week — better content depth but longer parent commit. Financial aid available.

items.label: California Science Center (LA Exposition Park)
items.detail: Member presale Feb 18-24, 2026; general enrollment after Feb 24. Mix-and-match morning + afternoon classes for full-day flexibility. Member: $225 half-day / $450 full-day. Extended care +$110-120/wk; member rate saves $10/wk.

sections.title: Pricing tiers for K-8 enrichment (2026 reference)

items.label: Free / fully-subsidized
items.detail: PSC scholarships (up to 100%, application opens Feb 6), SPS Expanded Learning, NSBE SEEK (3-week virtual), Black Girls CODE Summer Camp (most participants pay $0), CYC SF, LA's BEST, Audubon Junior Birder, Khan Academy, Code.org, Camp Wonderopolis (NCFL-funded). Many YMCAs use sliding scale 'Price A/Price B' self-selected by household income.

items.label: Low ($200-300/wk)
items.detail: Camp Invention $245-295 with promo codes (CIFUN25 by 3/31, CIFUN20 by 4/28). CodeWizardsHQ $200-300 1-week themed online. Camp CrunchLabs $329 for 12-week summer Build Box subscription (~$27/wk). Most municipal parks dept day camps $150-300/wk subsidized.

items.label: Mid ($400-600/wk)
items.detail: Destination Science $400. Camp Galileo Bellevue (varies, typical $500/wk). Camp Tech Revolution $500. Music Works NW $530. Birch Aquarium $250-600 range. Northwestern CTD half-day starts $395.

items.label: Premium ($600-1100/wk)
items.detail: Lawrence Hall $625-950/wk (2-week sessions). AMNH Discovery Squad $575-650. Exploratorium $675-750. Field Museum $425-575 (1-week). iD Tech UW Seattle from $1099/wk. Lavner UW from $799/wk.

items.label: Specialty / residential ($2000+)
items.detail: Earthwatch Family Expeditions $2000-3500/wk + airfare (need-based aid via Ignite Awards covers up to 100%). iD Tech Academy 2-week overnight $4999+. Interlochen Junior $3500-5500/2-wk (need-based aid covers 30-100% for ~40% of campers). NYLF Pathways residential $1500.

items.label: Single-day specialty
items.detail: Burke Museum $90-100/day ($90 members; +$30 optional aftercare). Many museum 'mini-camp' options $50-150/day. Apple Camp at Apple Stores 100% free 90-min sessions Jul-Aug.

items.label: Hidden cost-leverage patterns parents should know
items.detail: (1) Member early-access at major museums = the highest-leverage piece — membership often pays for itself just from earlier access to popular camps. (2) Multi-week + sibling discounts often stack with Early Bird. (3) Scholarship windows often close mid-May — apply early. (4) Free school-district summer enrichment is often the best-kept secret in any local market — check district website starting March. (5) Steve & Kate's Camp auto-refunds unused day passes after summer (Bay Area + LA only). (6) AAUW Tech Trek runs $50 fee for what's normally a $1000+ residential STEM week (rising 8th-grade girls; teacher nomination).

items.label: Seattle proper
items.detail: Top picks: Pacific Science Center (member Feb 2 / general Feb 9, pay-by-May-1), Burke Museum (single-day camps; Dino Trackers Jul 13 confirmed), Museum of Flight ACE (Feb 20-21 reg, Jun 22 – Aug 28, K-3 sessions at capacity by April), Woodland Park Zoo (10 sessions Jun 22 – Aug 28, $585/wk, scholarships up to 100% in 20% increments), Seattle Aquarium Marine Camp (Pier 59, 5-day weekly Jun 22 – Aug 28), Seattle Children's Theatre Drama School (Seattle Center campus, ages 3.5-18), Music Center NW (north Seattle; Music Together camp verified Jul 20-24 $295). FREE: SPS Expanded Learning (May 1 deadline, kids under 60th percentile in math/reading), Lakeside LEEP (May 1 deadline, current 5th+8th graders only, 4-week free incl. transportation). items.label: Specialty — chronic-illness + disability-focused
items.detail: Camp Korey (Carnation, WA) is 100% FREE including travel + meals + medical care for kids with serious medical conditions — cancer, blood disorders, neurological conditions, etc. SeriousFun Children's Network founded by Paul Newman. Disease-specific weeks. Apply 4-6 months ahead. Friendship Circle WA chapters pair special-needs kids with peer 'buddies' year-round (free).

items.label: WA scholarship landscape — 5 underused funding sources
items.detail: (1) PSC up to 100% (apps Feb 6, separate from regular reg — apply to BOTH); (2) Woodland Park Zoo up to 100% in 20% increments based on income; (3) Camp Sealth Camperships especially generous for first-time campers; (4) Camp Galileo up to 75% need-based aid; (5) Pierce County resident scholarship pool at Point Defiance Zoo. ALL UNDER-APPLIED-FOR — most parents don't know they exist or don't apply. Email camp directly even after windows close — often more flexibility than published.

items.label: Selectivity tiers — what admit rate actually means
items.detail: Tier 1 (sub-5% admit, automatic narrative weight at top schools): RSI MIT, SSP, MITES, JKCSF Cooke Young Scholars. Tier 2 (5-15% admit, strong differentiator): SUMaC, Mathcamp, PROMYS, Garcia Summer at Stony Brook, COSMOS, NIH HS-SIP. Tier 3 (15-40% admit, well-respected academic): Duke TIP, JHU CTY, Northwestern CTD, Stanford Compass (formerly EPGY), AwesomeMath. Tier 4 (open enrollment, supplemental): Beast Academy, AoPS Online, Outschool, university 'experience' programs. AOs read tiers like resume bullets — Tier 1+2 carry real weight; Tier 3 is good context but not differentiating; Tier 4 is fine as enrichment but won't move the needle alone.

items.label: Critical 2026 application deadlines for free / merit-based programs
items.detail: RSI MIT (Jan 15 app, ~80 admits worldwide). SSP (Feb 15 app, two campuses ~70/each). MITES (Feb 1 app, ~85 admits). PROMYS (Apr 1 app, ~80 admits). Mathcamp (Apr 1 app, ~120 admits). SUMaC (Mar 15 app, two sessions ~80 total). COSMOS (Feb 9 app, four UC campuses ~700 total). NIH HS-SIP (Feb 16 app). Garcia Summer at Stony Brook (Apr 1 app). Most are FREE or near-free for accepted students — application barrier IS the gate, not money.

items.label: What admissions officers actually value at the program level
items.detail: (1) Real research outputs (papers, posters, conference talks) > attended a brand-name program but produced nothing. (2) Sustained engagement (multi-year) > single summer cherry-pick. (3) FREE competitive programs (RSI, SSP, MITES, PROMYS) carry MORE weight per dollar than expensive open-enrollment ones — they signal selection on merit, not parental ability to pay. (4) Demonstrated tier-up across years (Tier 4 in 9th → Tier 2 in 11th) shows growth. (5) Local-impact projects (founded a chapter, ran a tutoring program) often outweigh brand-name programs for selective schools — distinctiveness > prestige.

items.label: Common HS strategy mistakes
items.detail: (1) Stacking 8 weeks of $5K programs each summer — reads as frantic, not focused. AOs prefer 1-2 deep commitments + sustained ECs over a buffet. (2) Chasing 'name brands' (Harvard summer, Yale Young Global Scholars, etc. that are open enrollment) when content doesn't match the intended major. (3) Ignoring free competitive programs because the application takes 4-6 hours — that's the WHOLE POINT of the gate. (4) Front-loading 9th-10th with programs then dropping in 11th-12th to 'focus on grades' — AOs notice the disengagement. (5) Doing programs in interests that don't align with intended major — fragmentation is worse than focus.

items.label: Cost / value tiers for HS programs
items.detail: FREE (sponsored): RSI, SSP, MITES, MOSTEC, JKCSF, NIH HS-SIP, COSMOS (very low fee), Garcia Summer ($1.5K research stipend). LOW ($500-2K/wk): TIP, CTY 1-2 wk commuter; AoPS Academy in-person ($400-700/wk); MIT Beaver Works (online + Cambridge, free for accepted). MID ($2-4K/2-3 wk): SUMaC, Mathcamp, PROMYS (residential incl. room+board); Stanford Compass; CTD Northwestern. PREMIUM ($5K+ for 3-6 wk): Brown Pre-College, Columbia Summer Immersion, Yale Young Global Scholars, Cornell Summer College — these are mostly OPEN ENROLLMENT and AOs know it. Generally not worth the price for differentiation; better as enrichment if budget allows.

items.label: How to build a sequenced multi-year HS strategy
items.detail: Grade 9: explore + apply broadly (Tier 3-4 programs to discover passions). Grade 10: build sustained engagement (back to a Tier 3 program OR scale into Tier 2 application). Grade 11: stretch (Tier 1-2 application — RSI, SSP, MITES). Grade 12: capitalize on a continuing project, NOT a new program (depth over breadth — finishing an existing project signals focus). Treat each summer as a chapter, not a list of resume bullets. The narrative through-line ('I started doing X in 9th, deepened in 10th, took it competitive in 11th') is what moves AOs.

items.label: Regional / state-specific bonuses
items.detail: Many states have FULL TUITION programs for in-state residents: California (COSMOS for CA residents — heavily favored), Texas (Texas Governor's Honors Program), Pennsylvania (PGSP), Tennessee (GSST), Missouri (Missouri Scholars Academy). Apply to your state's flagship even if you're also applying nationally. Some are summer-of-rising-12, some 11. Check state Department of Education + 'Governor's Schools' nationwide listing.

items.label: Internship vs program — different strategy logic
items.detail: PROGRAMS = structured curriculum + faculty/instructor-led + clear time-bounded outcome. Best for academic depth signal. INTERNSHIPS = work product + real organizational responsibility + reference letters from non-academic adults. Best for career-focused schools (engineering, business, premed) and for kids who learn better by doing than by classroom. Most students should do BOTH — programs to deepen academic skill, internships to demonstrate application + work ethic. Single-track focus (only programs OR only internships) reads thin.

items.label: What changes when your kid hits 9th grade
items.detail: Three big shifts. (1) Programs are now BUILD-MY-COLLEGE-APP weighted — admissions readers see the cumulative summers grades 9-12 on the Common App Activities/Honors sections. So 'fun' fades and 'directional' grows. (2) Selectivity tiers harden — RSI/SSP/MITES/PROMYS/NIH HS-SIP become real targets but most have rising-11th-grade minimums (apply Dec-Feb of 10th grade for summer after 11th). (3) Aid moves to merit + need-blind from sliding-scale at K-8 community programs.

items.label: What to do in 7th-8th grade summers
items.detail: Skip the panic of 'getting ahead.' DO build skill stacks that survive into HS: (a) one math contest pipeline (MATHCOUNTS → AMC 8 → AMC 10/12), (b) one creative-output pipeline (Github portfolio, blog, art portfolio, music demos), (c) one sustained service or research commitment that can extend into HS. AOs trace back depth from senior-year application to 7th grade — they want to see the REAL story, not 'discovered passion at 16'.

items.label: Programs that smoothly bridge K-8 → HS
items.detail: AoPS (Beast Academy K-5 → AoPS Online 5+ → AoPS Academy or competition track) — same ecosystem, harder problems. Synthesis Tutor → Synthesis Teams → joining Ad Astra alumni network. Code.org (CS Fundamentals K-5 → CS Discoveries 6-10 → CS Principles AP). Outschool/Khan Academy provide year-round continuity. CTY/CTD give a multi-year academic-enrichment pipeline. NSBE SEEK 4-6 → NSBE Jr 6-12. Black Girls CODE 5-12 → BGC Tech Tour HS+ → BGC scholarships.

items.label: What rising 9th graders should be applying to in fall 2026
items.detail: For STEM-bound rising 9th: target first-summer-of-HS at Tier 3-4 — local university outreach (Cooper Union STEM Outreach, MIT Splash, Stanford Splash, UCLA REACH), state Governor's Schools (rising 11+ but worth flagging now), DOE STEM Volunteer Internship (rising 10+). For arts-bound: pre-portfolio summer programs at art schools (RISD Pre-College, Otis College Pre-College, MICA Early College). For pre-med: hospital volunteer programs apply spring of 9th for summer of 10th. For research-bound: start emailing local university professors NOW for unpaid research shadowing.

items.label: FREE fall-of-9th-grade actions that compound
items.detail: (1) Get on the QuestBridge College Prep Scholars (CPS) interest list (they target rising 11th but mailing list = early access). (2) Sign up for Hispanic Heritage Foundation LOFT or HSF if eligible. (3) Subscribe to the Microsoft / Google / GitHub HS programs newsletters. (4) Bank of America Student Leaders application opens fall of junior year — but read up on it now. (5) Find your state's Governor's Honors Academy (varies by state, usually rising 12).

items.label: WA-specific 9th-grade transition
items.detail: Seattle/Eastside students entering 9th grade should look at: WA STEM (statewide STEM mentorship pipeline), UW Engineering Discovery Days (free annual event), UW MESA program (ongoing through HS), WA Aerospace Joint Apprenticeship (rising 11+), Seattle MESA mentorship. Lakeside LEEP graduates have priority into Lakeside's 9-12 programs but ALSO flag this for high-school admissions consideration ('I attended a multi-summer program at Lakeside') — it carries weight.

items.label: What WAY-too-early thinking gets wrong
items.detail: Don't pile 'resume-builder' programs onto a middle-schooler who hasn't found their thing yet. Better: subsidize ONE genuine interest with depth + room to fail. AOs see through 7-program-summer kids with no through-line. The kid who did 5 summers of one music camp and made progressively harder pieces beats the kid who did 5 unrelated 'prestigious' programs. Time on task + visible growth > brand collection.
